q: A team's fraud-detection model performs well in validation but degrades in production three months after deployment, with input feature distributions visibly shifted. This is best described as:
b: Data drift (covariate shift)
explain: The input distribution changed after deployment — covariate/data drift. Concept drift would be the input-output relationship changing; overfitting and leakage would show up before or at validation.

q: Concept drift differs from data drift in that concept drift means:
b: The relationship between inputs and the target variable changes
c: The model weights decay over time
explain: Data drift: P(X) changes. Concept drift: P(y|X) changes — e.g. fraud patterns evolve even if inputs look the same. Both call for monitoring and retraining triggers.

q: In MLOps, a 'feature store' primarily solves the problem of:
b: Consistent, reusable feature computation across training and serving, avoiding training-serving skew
explain: A feature store centralises feature definitions so the same values are served offline (training) and online (inference), preventing training-serving skew and duplication across teams.

q: Training-serving skew is:
a: An imbalance between GPU and CPU workloads
b: A mismatch between how data is processed at training time and at inference time
c: Difference in latency between batch and streaming
explain: When preprocessing or feature logic differs between the training pipeline and the serving path, the model sees different data than it learned on — a leading production failure mode.

q: Which set of practices most directly defines 'CI/CD for machine learning' beyond classic software CI/CD?
b: Versioning of data and models, automated retraining pipelines, model validation gates, and controlled promotion to serving
explain: ML adds artifacts (data, models) and behaviours (statistical performance) to version and validate; the pipeline itself, not just code, is the deployable unit.

q: A 'golden set' (golden run) in LLM system evaluation is:
b: A curated, fixed set of inputs with reference outputs used to detect regressions across model or prompt changes
explain: Golden sets pin expected behaviour so any prompt, model or retrieval change can be regression-tested — the LLM equivalent of a snapshot test suite.

q: LLM-as-judge evaluation is best used with which safeguard, given its known weaknesses?
b: Calibration against human ratings and awareness of biases such as position and verbosity preference
explain: LLM judges show position bias, verbosity bias and self-preference; anchoring them with rubrics and periodic human calibration is standard practice.

q: Red-teaming an AI system means:
b: Adversarially probing the system to surface harmful, unsafe or policy-violating behaviour before and after deployment
c: Marking failed test cases in red
explain: Red-teaming is systematic adversarial testing (jailbreaks, harmful content elicitation, misuse scenarios). Art 55 AI Act requires it for systemic-risk GPAI models.

q: In a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) architecture, the generation model's answers are grounded primarily by:
b: Retrieving relevant documents at query time and inserting them into the model's context
explain: RAG separates knowledge (retrievable corpus) from reasoning (the model): retrieve, then generate conditioned on retrieved context — updating knowledge without retraining.

q: Which failure is specific to the retrieval half of a RAG pipeline?
b: Relevant documents never reaching the model because of poor chunking or embedding mismatch
explain: Retrieval quality (chunking granularity, embedding model fit, top-k, filters) determines what the generator sees; evaluation should measure retrieval (recall/precision) separately from generation (faithfulness).

q: Chunking strategy in RAG involves a trade-off between:
b: Small chunks (precise retrieval, lost context) and large chunks (more context, diluted relevance and wasted context window)
explain: Chunk size/overlap tunes retrieval precision vs contextual completeness; common mitigations include semantic chunking, hierarchical retrieval and parent-document expansion.

q: A vector database's core operation for RAG is:
b: Approximate nearest-neighbour search over embedding vectors
explain: Documents and queries are embedded into vectors; ANN indexes (e.g. HNSW) return semantically similar items at scale with sub-linear search cost.

q: Hybrid search in retrieval systems combines:
b: Dense (embedding) similarity with sparse lexical matching such as BM25
explain: Dense retrieval captures semantics, lexical search captures exact terms (IDs, names, jargon); fusing both (e.g. reciprocal rank fusion) is standard for robust retrieval.

q: A reranker in a retrieval pipeline:
b: Re-scores a candidate set from the first-stage retriever with a more accurate (and more expensive) model, typically a cross-encoder
explain: Two-stage retrieval: cheap recall-oriented first stage, then precise reranking of the top candidates — better relevance at acceptable cost.

q: When should fine-tuning be preferred over RAG?
b: When the goal is adapting style, format, or task behaviour rather than injecting frequently-changing factual knowledge
explain: Fine-tuning bakes in behaviour and form; RAG serves volatile or auditable knowledge. Fresh facts via fine-tuning require constant retraining and lose source traceability.

q: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA work by:
a: Retraining all weights at lower precision
b: Training small additional weight matrices (adapters) while freezing the base model
explain: LoRA inserts low-rank update matrices, cutting compute/memory and letting many task adapters share one frozen base model.

q: Quantisation of an LLM primarily trades:
a: Accuracy for lower memory footprint and faster, cheaper inference
b: Latency for security
explain: Reducing weight precision (e.g. FP16→INT8/INT4) shrinks memory and speeds inference with a usually small accuracy cost — a key lever for cost and edge deployment.

q: Knowledge distillation is:
b: Training a smaller 'student' model to reproduce the behaviour of a larger 'teacher' model
explain: Distillation transfers capability into a cheaper model — a standard build-time answer to inference cost and latency constraints.

q: In LLM inference, the KV cache exists to:
b: Reuse attention keys/values of already-processed tokens so each new token does not recompute the full sequence
explain: Autoregressive decoding reuses per-token attention state; KV-cache size grows with context length and is a main driver of inference memory cost.

q: An agentic AI system differs from a single LLM call chiefly by:
b: Iteratively planning, invoking tools, observing results and deciding next steps toward a goal
explain: Agents run a loop — reason, act (tool/API call), observe, repeat — which brings power and new failure modes (error compounding, runaway actions) requiring guardrails and human oversight.

q: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardises:
b: How AI applications connect to external tools, data sources and prompts through interoperable servers and clients
explain: MCP is an open protocol for tool/context interoperability between AI clients and servers — the 'USB port' pattern for agent integrations, relevant to the Annex II 'AI interoperability' item.

q: Function calling (tool use) in LLM APIs means the model:
a: Executes code inside the model weights
b: Emits a structured request matching a declared tool schema, which the application executes before returning the result to the model
explain: The model never executes anything itself; it produces structured intent, the application executes and feeds results back — the boundary where validation and authorisation must live.

q: Prompt injection is:
b: Adversarial instructions hidden in input or retrieved content that override the system's intended behaviour
explain: Direct (user input) or indirect (poisoned documents/web pages in RAG/agent contexts) injection is the top LLM application risk (OWASP LLM01); mitigations include privilege separation, output validation and treating retrieved content as data.

q: An agent with tool access processes an inbound email that contains hidden text instructing it to forward the mailbox to an attacker. The primary defence class is:
b: Least-privilege tool authorisation, human confirmation for consequential actions, and isolating untrusted content from instructions
explain: Indirect prompt injection cannot be reliably filtered away; architecture must assume the model can be fooled — cap privileges, gate irreversible actions, separate trust domains.

q: Guardrails in an LLM production system are:
b: Input/output controls around the model — content filters, schema validation, policy checks, PII redaction — independent of the model's own alignment
explain: Defence-in-depth: validate inputs, constrain outputs (schemas, classifiers, rules) and log decisions, because model behaviour alone cannot guarantee policy compliance.

q: Which metric pair correctly matches a RAG faithfulness evaluation?
a: BLEU for retrieval, ROUGE for generation
b: Retrieval: context recall/precision; generation: groundedness of claims in the retrieved context
explain: Evaluate the stages separately: did retrieval fetch the needed evidence, and does the answer stick to it (faithfulness/groundedness vs hallucination).

q: A public leaderboard benchmark shows a model scoring far better than it performs on your task. The most likely explanations include:
a: The benchmark is wrong by definition
b: Benchmark contamination in training data and distribution mismatch with your domain
explain: Contamination (test data leaked into training) and domain mismatch are why bespoke, held-out task evals — not public benchmarks — should drive model selection.

q: In classification with heavy class imbalance (1% positives), which metric is most misleading?
b: Recall
explain: Predicting 'negative' always yields 99% accuracy. Precision/recall (and PR-AUC) expose performance on the minority class that matters.

q: Precision measures:
a: Of all actual positives, how many were found
b: Of all predicted positives, how many are truly positive
explain: Precision = TP/(TP+FP); recall = TP/(TP+FN). The precision-recall trade-off is tuned via the decision threshold to match the cost of false alarms vs misses.

q: A/B testing a new model version in production against the current one, on live traffic split between them, is called:
b: Online experimentation (A/B test); a variant serving only a small share first is a canary release
explain: A/B compares business/quality metrics on real traffic; shadow mode runs the challenger on copies of traffic without serving its output — a safer first step.

q: Shadow (dark) deployment of a model means:
b: Running the new model on production inputs in parallel while only the incumbent's outputs are served
explain: Shadow mode measures real-world behaviour risk-free before any traffic switch — standard promotion practice for high-stakes models.

q: Model registry and experiment tracking systems (e.g. MLflow-style) primarily provide:
b: Versioned lineage from data and code to trained model artifacts, with stage transitions (staging/production) and reproducibility metadata
explain: The registry is the backbone of governed promotion: which model, trained on what, evaluated how, approved by whom — also what AI Act Art 11/12 documentation leans on.

q: Data lineage means:
b: Traceability of data from source through transformations to consumption, enabling audit and impact analysis
explain: Lineage answers 'where did this value come from and what depends on it' — foundational for debugging pipelines, governance and regulatory traceability.

q: Common dimensions of data quality include:
a: Accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness
b: Volume, velocity, variety
explain: The standard DQ dimensions; the 3Vs describe big-data scale, not quality. Data readiness for AI is explicitly in Annex II.

q: ETL and ELT differ in that ELT:
b: Loads raw data into the target platform first and transforms it there, leveraging the warehouse/lakehouse compute
explain: Modern cloud pipelines favour ELT: land raw data, then transform in-platform (SQL/Spark), keeping raw history and enabling reprocessing.

q: A data pipeline orchestrator (Airflow-style) chiefly provides:
b: Scheduled, dependency-aware execution of pipeline tasks (DAGs) with retries, backfills and monitoring
explain: Orchestration is the control plane of data/ML pipelines: DAG dependencies, retries, alerting, backfill — reliability machinery, not computation itself.

q: Idempotency in a data pipeline task means:
b: Running it multiple times with the same inputs produces the same end state, making retries and backfills safe
explain: Idempotent tasks are the precondition for safe automatic retries — a favourite scenario question in pipeline troubleshooting.

q: 'Data mesh' as an architecture concept advocates:
a: One central data team owning all data
b: Domain-oriented ownership of data as a product, with federated governance and self-serve platform infrastructure
explain: Data mesh decentralises ownership to domains (data-as-a-product) under federated computational governance — contrast with the centralised lake/warehouse team model.

q: A lakehouse architecture combines:
b: The low-cost open-format storage of a data lake with warehouse-style ACID transactions, schema management and SQL performance
explain: Table formats (Delta/Iceberg-style) add transactions and governance on top of object storage — one platform for BI and ML workloads.

q: In build-vs-buy decisions for an enterprise AI capability, the strongest argument for BUILDING is:
b: The capability is a strategic differentiator requiring proprietary data or deep integration that vendors cannot match
explain: Commodity capabilities → buy; differentiating capabilities on proprietary data/processes → build. Total cost of ownership, lock-in, and time-to-value complete the assessment.

q: When selecting a model for a production task, the methodologically soundest approach is:
b: Define task-specific evaluation criteria and test candidate models on a representative held-out set, weighing quality against latency and cost
explain: Model selection is an evidence exercise against your task and constraints (quality, latency, cost, privacy, hosting), not a leaderboard lookup.

q: Temperature in LLM sampling controls:
b: The randomness of token selection — lower is more deterministic, higher more diverse
explain: Temperature rescales the output distribution. Low values suit extraction/factual tasks; higher values suit ideation. It does not change what the model knows.

q: Hallucination in LLMs is best characterised as:
b: Fluent output that is unsupported by the input, retrieved context, or reality
explain: Confident unsupported claims. Mitigations: grounding via RAG, faithfulness evaluation, citation requirements, abstention ('I don't know') paths — reduction, not elimination.

q: Which is a MODEL-level attack rather than an application-level one?
a: Prompt injection via a retrieved web page
b: Membership inference and model extraction attacks
d: SQL injection in the app backend
explain: Membership inference (was this record in training data?) and extraction (cloning behaviour via queries) target the model itself; injection targets the application's instruction handling.

q: Data poisoning is:
a: Corrupting data at rest by disk failure
b: Deliberately manipulating training (or retrieval) data so the model learns attacker-chosen behaviour
explain: Poisoning can implant backdoors or degrade performance; AI Act Art 15 explicitly requires high-risk systems to be resilient to it. Supply-chain hygiene of datasets is the defence.

q: MLSecOps supply-chain risks specific to ML include:
b: Malicious pre-trained models and unsafe serialisation formats (e.g. pickle) executing code on load
explain: Model artifacts are executable supply-chain inputs: unsafe deserialisation, tampered weights, poisoned public datasets. Use safe formats (safetensors), signing and provenance.

q: Differential privacy provides:
b: A mathematical guarantee that a computation's output reveals little about any single individual's record, via calibrated noise
explain: DP bounds the influence of any one record (epsilon budget). Removing names is de-identification and vulnerable to re-identification; DP gives provable bounds.

q: Federated learning is characterised by:
a: Training on one central GPU cluster
b: Training across decentralised data holders that share model updates, not raw data
explain: Data stays local; only gradients/updates are aggregated. Reduces data-sharing barriers but has its own risks (update leakage) — relevant for privacy-preserving AI at EU scale.

q: SHAP and LIME are techniques for:
b: Post-hoc explanation of individual model predictions via feature attribution
explain: Both attribute a prediction to input features (SHAP with game-theoretic guarantees, LIME via local surrogates) — core tools for explainability duties and model debugging.

q: Demographic parity and equalised odds are:
b: Group fairness criteria that generally cannot all be satisfied simultaneously, forcing documented trade-offs
c: EU legal requirements naming specific metrics
explain: Fairness metrics conflict mathematically (impossibility results); the engineering duty is choosing, justifying and documenting the criterion fit for the context — the law names no metric.

q: A model card is:
b: Structured documentation of a model's intended use, training data, evaluation results, limitations and ethical considerations
explain: Model cards (and datasheets for datasets) are the transparency artifacts that AI Act technical documentation (Annex IV/XI) builds on.

q: The transformer architecture's core mechanism is:
b: Self-attention weighing relationships among all tokens in a sequence in parallel
c: Recurrent hidden states processed token by token
explain: Self-attention replaced recurrence, enabling parallel training over sequences and the scaling behaviour behind modern LLMs.

q: Pre-training, instruction tuning, and RLHF/preference alignment respectively give an LLM:
b: Broad next-token capability; the ability to follow task instructions; outputs shaped to human preferences and safety norms
explain: The standard three-stage recipe: self-supervised pre-training on large corpora, supervised instruction tuning, then preference optimisation (RLHF/DPO-style).

q: Which deployment pattern minimises the risk of an irreversible harmful action by an autonomous agent in production?
b: Human-in-the-loop approval gates for consequential/irreversible actions, with autonomous execution only for low-risk reversible steps
c: Running the agent twice and comparing
d: Limiting the agent to office hours
explain: Tiered autonomy by action risk is the operative meaning of 'human oversight' (AI Act Art 14) for agentic systems.

q: Observability for an LLM application should capture, at minimum:
b: Traces of prompts, retrieved context, tool calls, outputs, latency, token cost, and quality/safety signals per request
explain: LLM observability = request-level traces linking inputs, context, actions and outputs to cost and quality — the substrate for eval, debugging, drift and incident response.

q: Semantic caching in an LLM service means:
b: Reusing responses for queries that are semantically similar to previously answered ones, cutting cost and latency
explain: Cache keys are embeddings, not exact strings; combined with prompt caching (reusing the processed shared prefix), it is a main inference-cost lever.

q: For a latency-sensitive, high-volume classification task with modest complexity, the cost-optimal choice is usually:
a: The largest frontier model with chain-of-thought
b: A small model (or distilled/fine-tuned variant) meeting the quality bar, with the large model reserved for hard cases (cascading/routing)
explain: Model routing/cascades match capacity to difficulty — the standard architecture answer to inference cost and latency trade-offs in Annex II's 'technology watch' area.

q: A/B metrics look flat but the new model's offline eval was clearly better. A likely cause worth checking first is:
b: Offline eval distribution does not represent live traffic, or the online metric is diluted/underpowered for the affected segment
explain: Offline-online metric gaps usually mean unrepresentative eval sets or underpowered experiments — check exposure, segment-level effects and sample size before concluding.

q: An ML team lead planning the path from pilot to production should treat which item as the critical path?
a: Choosing a logo for the tool
b: Production-grade data pipelines, monitoring, rollback and support ownership — the operational scaffolding around the model
explain: Most AI pilots die at operationalisation, not modelling: data reliability, MLOps, ownership and lifecycle processes are what 'leading AI teams to production' means in Annex II.

q: Retraining cadence for a production model should be driven by:
a: A fixed yearly schedule regardless of signals
b: Monitored drift and performance degradation signals, with automated triggers and validation gates before promotion
explain: Retraining is a monitored, gated loop: detect drift/decay → retrain → validate against golden sets and fairness checks → controlled rollout. Continuous improvement per Annex II's product lifecycle item.

q: The AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) takes which regulatory approach?
a: A rights-based framework granting individuals enforceable AI rights
b: A risk-based product regulation in the New Legislative Framework style
c: A sector-by-sector licensing regime administered by the Commission
d: A voluntary code of conduct with optional certification
explain: The AI Act is risk-based product regulation (legal basis Art 114 TFEU, internal market), not a rights-based instrument. Obligations scale with the risk tier of the system.

q: The AI Act's definition of an 'AI system' (Art 3(1)) is deliberately aligned with which international definition?
b: The NIST AI RMF definition
d: The Council of Europe Framework Convention definition
explain: Art 3(1) mirrors the OECD definition: a machine-based system with varying autonomy that infers from input how to generate outputs influencing physical or virtual environments.

q: A US provider offers an AI system whose output is used by customers in the EU, without any EU establishment. Does the AI Act apply?
a: No — the Act applies only to providers established in the EU
b: Yes — the Act applies where the output produced by the system is used in the EU
c: Only if the provider processes EU personal data
d: Only after the provider appoints an EU representative
explain: Art 2 gives the Act extraterritorial reach: it covers providers placing systems on the EU market wherever established, and situations where the system's output is used in the EU.

q: Which of these is excluded from the AI Act's scope?
a: AI systems used by public authorities for border control
b: AI systems placed on the market for military and defence purposes
explain: Art 2 excludes military/defence/national-security uses, pure scientific R&D, and purely personal non-professional use. Border control is in scope (Annex III area 7).

q: An HR department deploys software that screens and ranks incoming CVs. Under the AI Act this system is:
b: High-risk under Annex III (employment)
c: Subject only to Art 50 transparency duties
explain: Recruitment and screening tools fall under Annex III area 4 (employment and worker management), making the system high-risk — allowed, but subject to Arts 8–15 requirements and conformity assessment.

q: Real-time remote biometric identification (RBI) in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement is:
b: Prohibited, with three narrow exceptions requiring prior judicial or independent administrative authorisation
d: Permitted with notification to the market surveillance authority
explain: Art 5(1)(h) bans it except for targeted victim/missing-person searches, specific imminent threats (incl. terrorism), and locating suspects of serious offences — each needing prior authorisation under Art 5(3).

q: Retrospective (post) remote biometric identification by police from recorded CCTV footage is:
b: High-risk under Annex III with specific safeguards in Art 26(10)
explain: A classic trap: only REAL-TIME RBI for law enforcement is (conditionally) prohibited. Post RBI is high-risk (Annex III 1(a)) with deployer safeguards, not banned.

q: Emotion recognition systems are prohibited by the AI Act in which settings?
b: Workplaces and education institutions, except for medical or safety reasons
d: They are never prohibited, only high-risk
explain: Art 5(1)(f) bans emotion inference in the workplace and education institutions, with a medical/safety carve-out. Elsewhere emotion recognition may be high-risk (Annex III 1) plus Art 50 disclosure.

q: Which practice is prohibited by Art 5?
a: Predicting an individual's risk of committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or personality traits
b: AI-assisted analysis of objective evidence supporting a human assessment of criminal risk
explain: Art 5(1)(d) bans purely profiling-based individual crime prediction. Supporting a human assessment grounded in objective facts is allowed; credit scoring and proctoring are high-risk, not banned.

q: Untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV to build a facial-recognition database is:
b: Allowed with a DPIA
explain: Art 5(1)(e) prohibits untargeted scraping to create or expand facial-recognition databases — the Clearview-style scenario — for any actor.

q: A city government scores residents over time on social behaviour and unrelated personal traits, and denies benefits to low scorers. This is:
b: Prohibited social scoring under Art 5(1)(c)
d: Outside the Act because it is a public body
explain: Social scoring producing detrimental treatment that is unjustified, disproportionate or unrelated to the original context is banned — for public AND private actors.

q: The Digital Omnibus on AI (Reg. (EU) 2026/1744) added a new prohibited practice to Art 5, namely:
b: AI systems for producing non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material
explain: The 2026 Omnibus added the NCII/CSAM-generation prohibition, with its own transition running to 2 December 2026.

q: Under Art 6(1), an AI system is high-risk when it is:
b: A safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation law requiring third-party conformity assessment
c: Any system deployed by a public authority
explain: Art 6(1) covers AI as a safety component of (or itself) a regulated product — machinery, toys, medical devices, vehicles. Art 6(2) covers stand-alone Annex III systems.

q: The Art 6(3) filter lets an Annex III system escape high-risk classification — except that classification always remains high-risk when the system:
b: Performs profiling of natural persons
explain: Art 6(3) exempts narrow procedural/preparatory tasks, but profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, and using the filter must be documented (with registration of the claim for Annex III systems).

q: Which is NOT one of the eight Annex III high-risk areas?
b: Migration, asylum and border control
d: Administration of justice and democratic processes
explain: The eight areas: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration/border, justice/democracy. Marketing is not among them.

q: Creditworthiness scoring of natural persons falls under which Annex III area?
b: Essential private and public services
explain: Annex III area 5 covers access to essential services: public benefits eligibility, credit scoring, life/health insurance risk pricing, and emergency-call dispatching.

q: Art 10 of the AI Act imposes requirements on high-risk systems concerning:
b: Training, validation and testing data governance and quality, including bias examination
explain: Art 10 is the data-and-data-governance article: relevant, representative, error-checked datasets and examination for possible biases. Human oversight is Art 14; CE marking Art 48.

q: Art 14 (human oversight) requires for remote biometric identification specifically:
b: Verification of the result by at least two natural persons
c: Monthly audits by a notified body
explain: Art 14(5): no action on a high-risk biometric identification unless separately verified and confirmed by at least two competent natural persons.

q: Art 15 requires high-risk AI systems to be resilient against which AI-specific attacks?
b: Data poisoning, model evasion and adversarial examples
explain: Art 15 names accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, explicitly including resistance to data poisoning, model poisoning/evasion and adversarial inputs — product-level AI security.

q: The default conformity assessment route for an Annex III high-risk system (e.g. a recruitment tool) is:
a: Third-party assessment by a notified body, always
b: Internal control (self-assessment) under Annex VI
explain: Internal control is the default. A notified body is required only for Annex III point 1 biometrics when harmonised standards are not fully applied, and per sectoral law for Annex I products.

q: Applying harmonised standards published in the OJ gives a high-risk provider:
b: A presumption of conformity with the corresponding requirements
explain: Art 40: conformity with harmonised standards creates a presumption of conformity — the standard NLF mechanism, and why CEN-CENELEC JTC 21 standards matter so much.

q: Which sequence correctly orders provider duties before placing a high-risk system on the market?
b: Conformity assessment → EU declaration of conformity → CE marking → registration in the EU database
d: EU declaration of conformity alone suffices
explain: Assessment (Art 43) precedes the declaration (Art 47), the CE mark (Art 48) and registration (Arts 49/71). Getting the order right is a favourite MCQ pattern.

q: A provider must report a serious incident with a high-risk system to the market surveillance authority within:
b: 72 hours
c: 15 days (2 days for widespread infringement or critical infrastructure)
explain: Art 73: 15 days as the general rule, shortened to 2 days for widespread infringements or serious incidents involving critical infrastructure — distinguish from GDPR's 72-hour breach rule.

q: Deployers of high-risk AI systems must keep the automatically generated logs for at least:
b: 6 months
explain: Art 26: deployers keep logs at least six months (unless other Union/national law says more). Providers keep technical documentation 10 years — don't confuse the two.

q: A bank buys a third-party AI credit-scoring system, puts its own brand on it and substantially modifies the model. Under Art 25 the bank:
b: Becomes the provider, assuming provider obligations
c: Needs only to inform the original provider
d: Is exempt because it is a financial institution
explain: Rebranding, substantial modification, or repurposing a system so it becomes high-risk shifts provider obligations onto the modifier — the value-chain rule of Art 25.

q: A fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA, Art 27) before first use of a high-risk system is required from:
a: All deployers of any AI system
b: Providers only
c: Public bodies, private entities providing public services, and deployers of credit-scoring and life/health insurance pricing systems
explain: Art 27 targets those three deployer groups (critical infrastructure excepted). The FRIA can build on an existing GDPR DPIA (Art 27(4)).

q: Under Art 86, a person affected by a decision based on a high-risk Annex III system has the right to:
b: Obtain a clear and meaningful explanation of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure
explain: Art 86 creates the explanation right for affected persons — an individual-rights element in an otherwise product-safety law.

q: Under Art 50, which does NOT carry a transparency obligation?
b: AI-generated deepfake video content
c: Synthetic audio content published for artistic purposes
explain: Art 50 covers interaction disclosure (chatbots), machine-readable marking of synthetic content, and deepfake labelling (with a limited artistic-work regime). Spam filters are minimal-risk.

q: The Art 4 AI-literacy obligation requires:
a: All EU citizens to pass an AI test
b: Providers and deployers to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy in their staff dealing with AI systems
c: Member States to add AI to school curricula
explain: Art 4 (applicable since 2 Feb 2025) puts the literacy duty on providers and deployers for their own staff and operators — often overlooked because it sits outside the high-risk chapter.

q: A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have systemic risk when cumulative training compute exceeds:
b: 10^24 FLOPs
explain: Art 51: >10^25 floating-point operations triggers the presumption; the Commission can also designate models per Annex XIII criteria. Providers must notify the Commission within 2 weeks of meeting it.

q: ALL GPAI model providers must, under Art 53:
b: Maintain technical documentation, provide information to downstream providers, adopt a copyright policy, and publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training content
explain: The four baseline GPAI duties. The training-content summary follows the AI Office template published in July 2025.

q: The open-source exemption for GPAI models does NOT relieve providers from:
b: Downstream information duties
c: The copyright policy and the training-content summary
explain: Free and open-licence models with public weights skip the two documentation duties, but copyright policy and training summary always apply — and the whole exemption vanishes for systemic-risk models.

q: Providers of GPAI models WITH systemic risk must additionally (Art 55):
b: Perform state-of-the-art model evaluations including adversarial testing, mitigate systemic risks, report serious incidents to the AI Office, and ensure cybersecurity of model and infrastructure
explain: The four Art 55 duties: evaluation/red-teaming, risk mitigation, incident reporting, cybersecurity protection.

q: The GPAI Code of Practice (published 10 July 2025) is best described as:
b: A voluntary compliance vehicle (chapters: Transparency, Copyright, Safety & Security) giving an adequate way to demonstrate compliance until harmonised standards exist
explain: Signing is voluntary; the Commission and Member States confirmed it as an adequate compliance tool. The Safety & Security chapter applies only to systemic-risk model providers.

q: The GPAI copyright policy obligation (Art 53(1)(c)) hooks into which existing EU law?
b: The text-and-data-mining opt-out in Art 4(3) of the DSM Copyright Directive (EU) 2019/790
explain: GPAI providers must identify and respect TDM reservations of rights — the legal bridge between AI training and EU copyright law.

q: Which body exclusively supervises and enforces the GPAI model obligations?
b: The European Data Protection Supervisor
explain: GPAI enforcement is centralised at the AI Office (fines up to €15m/3% under Art 101). National authorities enforce everything else — a high-yield distinction.

q: The European AI Board (Art 65) is composed of:
b: One representative per Member State
explain: One rep per Member State (EDPS as observer), advising and coordinating national implementation — the EDPB analogue. Stakeholders sit in the Advisory Forum (Art 67) instead.

q: The Scientific Panel of independent experts (Art 68) can:
b: Issue qualified alerts to the AI Office about systemic risks of GPAI models
explain: The Panel (formally established 1 June 2026, up to 60 experts) supports the AI Office on GPAI and can trigger qualified alerts that may lead to systemic-risk designation.

q: Each Member State must designate as national competent authorities:
b: At least one notifying authority and at least one market surveillance authority
explain: Art 70: notifying authority (accredits notified bodies) + market surveillance authority (enforcement), one acting as single point of contact. Deadline was 2 Aug 2025 — many Member States missed it.

q: Regulatory sandboxes under the AI Act:
b: Must exist in every Member State — at least one operational by 2 August 2026
c: Are run exclusively by the AI Office
explain: Art 57 obliges each Member State to have at least one AI regulatory sandbox (possibly jointly with others) by 2 Aug 2026; real-world testing is governed by Arts 60–61.

q: The maximum fine for engaging in a prohibited practice (Art 5) is:
a: €15 m or 3% of worldwide annual turnover
b: €35 m or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
explain: The top bracket. Most other operator breaches: €15m/3%; misleading information to authorities: €7.5m/1%. For SMEs the LOWER of the amounts applies.

q: Fines for EU institutions and bodies violating the AI Act are imposed by:
b: The European Data Protection Supervisor
explain: Art 100: the EDPS fines EU institutions (up to €1.5m for prohibited practices). A niche fact exam writers like because the obvious answer (AI Office) is wrong.

q: Which AI Act provisions have applied since 2 February 2025?
b: Prohibitions (Art 5) and the AI-literacy duty (Art 4)
explain: The first application wave. GPAI rules, governance and penalties followed on 2 Aug 2025; Art 50 transparency on 2 Aug 2026.

q: After the Digital Omnibus, obligations for stand-alone Annex III high-risk systems apply from:
b: 2 February 2027
explain: The Omnibus (Reg. (EU) 2026/1744) moved Annex III high-risk from 2 Aug 2026 to a fixed 2 Dec 2027, and Annex I embedded/product high-risk to 2 Aug 2028. Pre-Omnibus materials are outdated — a top trap.

q: Which obligation stayed on its original schedule despite the Digital Omnibus deferrals?
b: Annex I product-embedded high-risk obligations
explain: Chatbot disclosure, machine-readable marking of synthetic content and deepfake labelling applied on 2 Aug 2026 as planned (legacy generative systems: grace until 2 Dec 2026).

q: Legacy GPAI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by:
b: 2 August 2026
explain: Two-year runway for pre-existing models. Distinguish from legacy high-risk systems of public authorities (2030).

q: A high-risk provider processing special categories of personal data strictly to detect and correct bias relies on:
a: A GDPR Art 9 blanket ban — it is impossible
b: AI Act Art 10(5), which permits it under strict safeguards
explain: Art 10(5) creates a narrow legal gateway for sensitive-data processing for bias correction — a classic AI Act/GDPR interplay question.

q: The relationship between the AI Act and the GDPR is best described as:
a: The AI Act replaces the GDPR for AI systems
b: They apply in parallel: the AI Act adds product-safety duties, the GDPR governs the lawfulness of personal-data processing
c: The GDPR only applies to non-AI processing
d: The AI Act is lex specialis ousting the GDPR
explain: Complementary regimes. A compliant high-risk system still needs a GDPR lawful basis; a FRIA can build on a DPIA.

q: AI Act Art 15 cybersecurity and NIS2 differ in that:
b: Art 15 is product-level security of the high-risk AI system; NIS2 is organisation-level security for essential/important entities
d: Art 15 applies to networks, NIS2 to software
explain: Product vs organisation is the standard one-liner; the Cyber Resilience Act (products with digital elements) can support the Art 15 presumption.

q: After the Commission withdrew the AI Liability Directive proposal in February 2025, liability for defective AI in the EU rests primarily on:
b: The new Product Liability Directive (2024), which treats software including AI as a 'product' under strict liability
explain: The revised PLD covers AI as a product with strict liability for defects; the fault-based AI Liability Directive was withdrawn, so no AI-specific fault instrument exists.

q: The seven requirements of the HLEG Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI include:
b: Human agency and oversight; technical robustness and safety; privacy and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; societal and environmental well-being; accountability
explain: The 2019 HLEG list of seven — the pre-AI-Act ethical framework the exam may still reference; trustworthy AI = lawful, ethical, robust.

q: ISO/IEC 42001 specifies:
a: A risk taxonomy for ML models
b: Requirements for an AI management system (AIMS) that organisations can certify against
explain: 42001 is the management-system standard (the 'ISO 27001 of AI'); ISO/IEC 23894 is AI risk-management guidance. Both support AI Act conformity work.

q: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organises its functions as:
b: Govern – Map – Measure – Manage
explain: The four AI RMF functions. 'Identify–Protect–…' is the NIST Cybersecurity Framework — a deliberate distractor.

q: Under the GDPR, a decision based solely on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects:
a: Is always lawful with a privacy notice
b: Is restricted by Art 22, requiring a valid basis (contract, law, or explicit consent) and safeguards including human intervention
d: Falls only under the AI Act
explain: GDPR Art 22 is the automated-decision rule that overlaps with Annex III systems (credit, recruitment); the AI Act adds Art 86's explanation right for high-risk decisions.

q: A deployer notices a high-risk system presents a risk under Art 26. It must:
b: Suspend use and inform the provider and the market surveillance authority without undue delay
explain: Deployer duties include monitoring, suspension on risk, informing provider/distributor and the authority — plus informing workers before workplace use, and verifying database registration for public bodies.

q: Providers of high-risk AI systems must keep technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity at the disposal of authorities for:
b: 3 years
c: 10 years after the system is placed on the market
explain: Art 18: ten years. Pairs with (and contrasts against) the deployer's 6-month log-retention floor.

q: Market surveillance of AI systems operates under which framework regulation?
a: Reg. (EU) 2019/1020 on market surveillance and compliance of products
b: The GDPR
explain: The AI Act plugs into the general product market-surveillance regime of Reg. 2019/1020; fundamental-rights bodies also get document access for rights-related high-risk systems (Art 77).

q: An 'AI system' tier and a 'GPAI model' classification relate how?
b: They are parallel tracks: the model has Chapter V duties, while a system built on it gets its own risk tier
explain: A chatbot built on a GPAI model can be minimal/limited risk while the underlying model carries Art 53/55 duties — model vs system is a foundational distinction.

q: Which statement about SME penalties under the AI Act is correct?
b: SMEs face the same brackets, but the LOWER of the percentage or fixed amount applies
d: Only the Commission may fine SMEs
explain: Art 99(6): same infringement categories, capped at the lower of the two amounts — the Omnibus also extended SME simplifications to 'small mid-cap' companies.

q: The provider of a GPAI model that meets the systemic-risk compute threshold must notify the Commission within:
b: 2 weeks
explain: Art 52: notification without delay and in any event within two weeks of meeting (or learning it will meet) the Art 51 threshold.

q: The European AI Office is administratively located in:
b: The Commission's DG CNECT (Communications Networks, Content and Technology)
explain: Established by Commission Decision of 24 January 2024, the AI Office sits within DG CNECT and provides Union-level AI expertise, GPAI enforcement and codes of practice.

q: The AI Act Scientific Panel of independent experts was formally established in June 2026 with:
a: Up to 60 independent experts on two-year renewable terms
b: 27 national ministers
explain: Implementing Reg. (EU) 2025/454; panel launched 1 June 2026 — up to 60 experts, at least one per EU/EFTA/EEA state (max 3 per state). It advises the AI Office and can issue qualified alerts on GPAI systemic risk.

q: By its 2 August 2025 deadline, designation of national competent authorities under the AI Act was:
b: Widely missed — only a minority of Member States had designated both required authorities
explain: Implementation lags: by early 2026 only around 9 Member States had designated both market-surveillance and notifying authorities — context the exam may probe as 'state of implementation'.

q: The GPAI Code of Practice's three chapters are:
b: Transparency, Copyright, and Safety & Security
explain: Published 10 July 2025. Transparency and Copyright apply to all GPAI providers; Safety & Security only to providers of systemic-risk models (>10^25 FLOPs).

q: Full Commission enforcement powers over GPAI obligations (fines, requests for information, model access) apply from:
b: 2 August 2026, after a one-year grace period from the obligations' start
explain: GPAI obligations applied from 2 Aug 2025, but the AI Act gave the Commission enforcement tools a year later — from 2 Aug 2026.

q: The Digital Omnibus on AI (Reg. (EU) 2026/1744) entered into force in:
b: July 2026, following Council approval on 29 June 2026
explain: Published in the OJ on 24 July 2026, in force 27 July 2026. It defers Annex III high-risk to 2 Dec 2027 and Annex I to 2 Aug 2028, adds the NCII/CSAM prohibition, and introduces simplifications including the 'small mid-cap' category.

q: Besides the AI Act, the Digital Omnibus on AI also amended:
a: The GDPR and the ePrivacy Directive
b: The EASA Basic Regulation (2018/1139) and the Machinery Regulation (2023/1230)
explain: The Omnibus aligned sectoral product law (aviation, machinery) with the deferred AI high-risk timelines — it did not touch the GDPR, DSA or DMA.

q: The 'small mid-cap' (SMC) category introduced by the Digital Omnibus matters because:
a: SMCs are exempt from the AI Act entirely
b: It extends SME-style simplified documentation and compliance burdens to companies somewhat larger than SMEs
c: It creates a new tax bracket
explain: Part of the Commission's simplification agenda: proportionate obligations for small mid-caps alongside SMEs, e.g. simplified technical documentation.

q: The Data Act (Reg. (EU) 2023/2854) became applicable on:
b: 1 January 2024
explain: The Data Act applies from 12 Sept 2025: IoT/connected-product data access for users, business-to-business sharing terms, cloud switching. 'Data by design' duties for new products follow from 12 Sept 2026.

q: The Data Act chiefly regulates:
b: Access to and sharing of data generated by connected products and related services, plus cloud switching and unfair contractual terms
explain: It gives users of connected products rights over generated data, sets FRAND-style sharing conditions, and eases switching between data-processing services — complementing, not replacing, the GDPR.

q: The Data Governance Act (Reg. (EU) 2022/868) established:
b: Frameworks for re-use of protected public-sector data, notified data intermediation services, and data altruism organisations
explain: The DGA (applicable since Sept 2023) is the trust framework: public-sector data re-use, neutral data intermediaries, and altruistic data donation — infrastructure for the common European data spaces.

q: Common European data spaces are:
b: Sector-specific federated data-sharing ecosystems (health, mobility, energy, agriculture…) built on common governance and interoperability rules
c: Cloud regions operated by US providers
explain: The European data strategy's flagship: sectoral data spaces (with EHDS the first legislated one) to make data flow within trusted EU frameworks — key training-data context for AI policy.

q: The European Health Data Space Regulation (Reg. (EU) 2025/327):
b: Entered into force in March 2025, enabling primary use (patient access, cross-border) and secondary use of health data for research, with main secondary-use provisions applying around 2029
d: Replaces the GDPR for health data
explain: EHDS is the first sectoral data space in law: in force 26 March 2025, phased application (secondary-use core ~March 2029; some data categories 2031).

q: The DSA and the AI Act divide labour how?
a: They regulate the same thing twice
b: The DSA regulates online platforms/intermediaries (moderation, recommender transparency, VLOP systemic risk); the AI Act regulates AI systems themselves wherever deployed
c: The DSA is only for social media ads
d: The AI Act supersedes the DSA
explain: Platform duties vs product duties. A VLOP's recommender falls under DSA systemic-risk rules; the same company's AI system obligations come from the AI Act.

q: Under the DSA, 'VLOP' designation means:
b: A platform with over 45 million average monthly active EU users, subject to systemic-risk assessment, audits and data access for researchers
c: A platform with over 1 billion global users
explain: 45m ≈ 10% of the EU population. Around 17+ VLOPs designated; ChatGPT was designated as a Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE) — an AI-relevant DSA first.

q: The DMA regulates 'gatekeepers', which as of 2026 include:
b: Seven designated companies: Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Booking.com, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft
explain: The DMA imposes ex-ante do's and don'ts (interoperability, no self-preferencing, data-combination limits) on designated core platform services of these seven gatekeepers.

q: NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) required Member State transposition by:
a: 17 October 2024 — a deadline many Member States missed, leading to infringement action and CJEU referrals in 2026
b: 2 August 2025
d: It is directly applicable and needs no transposition
explain: NIS2 is a directive (unlike the AI Act). Transposition was due 17 Oct 2024; in July 2026 the Commission referred several Member States to the CJEU for failure to transpose.

q: NIS2 applies to:
b: 'Essential' and 'important' entities in critical sectors (energy, transport, health, digital infrastructure…), imposing organisational cybersecurity risk management and incident reporting
explain: Organisation-level cybersecurity across 18 sectors with management accountability and 24h/72h incident reporting — complementary to product-level rules (AI Act Art 15, CRA).

q: The Cyber Resilience Act (Reg. (EU) 2024/2847) covers:
b: Cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements across their lifecycle, with CE marking; main obligations fully applicable 11 December 2027
explain: CRA = product cybersecurity (secure-by-design, vulnerability handling, updates). In force 10 Dec 2024; reporting duties phase in 2026, full application 11 Dec 2027. Meeting CRA requirements supports AI Act Art 15 conformity.

q: The Digital Decade Policy Programme 2030 sets which target for ICT specialists in the EU?
b: 10 million
explain: 2030 targets: 20m ICT specialists (with gender convergence), 80% of adults with basic digital skills, 75% of EU companies using cloud/AI/big data, gigabit connectivity for all, 100% key public services online.

q: The Digital Decade target for enterprise AI uptake is:
b: 75% of EU companies using cloud, AI or big data by 2030
explain: The 75% cloud/AI/big-data uptake target is the business-digitalisation pillar; annual State of the Digital Decade reports track (and show gaps against) it.

q: The AI Continent Action Plan (April 2025) is built around:
b: Compute infrastructure (AI Factories and Gigafactories), data, skills, sectoral adoption and simplification — to make the EU a leading 'AI continent'
explain: Announced 9 April 2025: scaling EuroHPC-based AI Factories, up to 5 AI Gigafactories, data-union strategy, skills, and the Apply AI adoption push.

q: AI Factories are:
b: AI-optimised supercomputing hubs built around EuroHPC machines, giving startups, SMEs and researchers access to compute, data and talent services
d: Private US cloud regions in the EU
explain: 19+ AI Factories selected across Member States under EuroHPC JU — the EU's answer to compute access for its AI ecosystem; Gigafactories (~100k+ advanced AI chips) are the next scale step.

q: InvestAI aims to mobilise approximately:
b: €20 billion total
c: €200 billion for AI investment, including a ~€20 billion fund for AI gigafactories
explain: Announced at the February 2025 AI Action Summit in Paris: €200bn overall mobilisation with a €20bn public-private gigafactory facility; the EuroHPC gigafactory call followed in July 2026.

q: The Apply AI Strategy (October 2025) focuses on:
b: Accelerating AI adoption in strategic EU sectors and the public sector, with about €1 billion mobilised and an 'AI first' policy push
explain: COM(2025)724, presented 8 Oct 2025 alongside the AI in Science strategy: sectoral adoption (health, manufacturing, energy…), Apply AI Alliance, ~€1bn from existing programmes.

q: The EU's AI in Science strategy includes RAISE, which is:
a: A new tax on AI companies
b: A (pilot) virtual European institute pooling resources to attract and support AI talent in science
explain: RAISE (Resource for AI Science in Europe) pilots pooling compute/data/talent for AI-driven research, funded via Horizon Europe — part of the Oct 2025 strategy package.

q: The Coordinated Plan on AI is:
b: A joint Commission-Member States framework (2018, revised 2021) aligning national AI strategies and investment, targeting €20bn/year of AI investment this decade
explain: Soft-coordination instrument predating the AI Act; most Member States now have national AI strategies under it. Progress is reviewed jointly with the OECD.

q: EuroHPC Joint Undertaking is:
b: The EU body pooling EU and national funding to procure and operate world-class supercomputers — now also mandated to host AI Factories and Gigafactories
explain: EuroHPC JU (machines like LUMI, Leonardo, JUPITER — the EU's first exascale system) had its mandate extended in 2026 to the AI gigafactory programme.

q: The AI Act's national regulatory sandboxes are intended primarily to:
b: Let providers, especially SMEs and startups, develop and test innovative AI under regulatory supervision before market placement
explain: Art 57: at least one sandbox per Member State by 2 Aug 2026, with priority SME access — the innovation-support counterweight to the Act's obligations.

q: Which body issues opinions and coordinates consistent AI Act application across Member States?
b: ENISA
explain: The AI Board (one representative per Member State, Art 65) coordinates national implementation and advises the Commission — with the Advisory Forum providing stakeholder input.

q: The Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (2024) differs from the AI Act in that it:
a: Regulates products for the internal market
b: Is an international human-rights treaty on AI open to non-European states, setting principles rather than product-conformity rules
explain: The CoE Convention (signed by the EU, US, UK among others) is rights-principles-based international law; the AI Act is detailed internal-market product regulation.

q: The GDPR's role in the EU AI landscape is best summarised as:
b: The horizontal personal-data layer: lawful basis, purpose limitation, data-subject rights and DPIAs apply to AI training and use whenever personal data is processed
explain: EDPB opinions address AI-model training and lawful basis; the AI Act repeatedly defers to the GDPR — exam questions like testing that both apply cumulatively.

q: Standardisation supporting the AI Act is led by:
b: CEN and CENELEC (notably JTC 21) under a Commission standardisation request, producing harmonised European standards that give presumption of conformity
explain: European harmonised standards (hENs), once cited in the OJ, trigger the Art 40 presumption of conformity — why the delayed JTC 21 work programme matters to the whole timeline.

q: ENISA is:
b: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity — supporting NIS2 implementation, certification schemes and cyber preparedness
explain: ENISA anchors the cybersecurity side (NIS2, EU cybersecurity certification under the Cybersecurity Act) — adjacent to, but distinct from, AI Act governance.

q: The EU's approach to general-purpose AI risk is internationally distinctive because it:
b: Imposes binding legal obligations on GPAI providers (transparency, copyright, systemic-risk duties) where most jurisdictions rely on voluntary commitments
explain: Chapter V is the first binding GPAI regime; the US executive-order/voluntary approach and UK safety-institute model contrast with it — a classic comparative-policy question.

q: 'Digital sovereignty' / 'strategic autonomy' in EU AI policy refers to:
b: Reducing critical dependencies (chips, cloud, foundation models) and building EU capacity — compute, data, talent — while remaining open
explain: The motivation behind the Chips Act, EuroHPC/AI Factories, InvestAI and data-space policy: capacity and resilience, not isolation.

q: The European Chips Act aims to:
b: Double the EU's share of global semiconductor production toward 20% by 2030 through public-private investment and fab support
explain: Semiconductors are the compute substrate of AI policy; the Chips Act (2023) is the supply-side complement to AI Factories and Gigafactories.

q: Under the AI Act, deepfake labelling obligations (Art 50) sit in EU disinformation policy alongside:
b: The DSA's systemic-risk duties for VLOPs and the (strengthened) Code of Practice/Conduct on Disinformation
explain: Synthetic-content transparency (AI Act) + platform risk mitigation (DSA) + the disinformation code integrated into the DSA co-regulatory framework — the layered EU answer to AI-driven disinformation.

q: The 'Brussels effect' in AI policy describes:
b: EU rules becoming de facto global standards as multinational providers align worldwide products with the strictest major market
explain: As with the GDPR, the AI Act's extraterritorial reach and market size push global compliance alignment — a standard policy-analysis concept the essay or MCQ can invoke.

q: AI literacy policy in the EU (AI Act Art 4 plus skills programmes) is supported financially mainly by:
b: Digital Europe Programme, Horizon Europe and related instruments funding digital skills, research and deployment
explain: DIGITAL (deployment, skills, AI testing facilities) and Horizon Europe (research) are the twin funding arms behind the Digital Decade skills targets.

q: Which statement about the AI Act's essay-worthy 'innovation vs regulation' debate is factually accurate as of 2026?
a: The EU abandoned the AI Act
b: The Commission pursued simplification (Digital Omnibus deferrals, SME/SMC relief) while keeping prohibitions and transparency on schedule — responding to competitiveness critiques like the Draghi report
explain: The 2026 policy story: burden-reduction and deadline deferral for high-risk compliance, paired with unchanged fundamentals — framed by the Draghi competitiveness report's critique of regulatory load.

q: The EDPS's AI-related role includes:
b: Supervising EU institutions' own compliance — including acting as their market surveillance authority under the AI Act and imposing fines under Art 100
explain: The EDPS wears two hats: data-protection supervisor of EU institutions and their AI Act surveillance authority — while national authorities and the AI Office cover everyone else.

q: 'High-impact' international AI safety cooperation the EU participates in includes:
b: AI safety summits/network of safety institutes, the G7 Hiroshima Process code of conduct, and OECD AI work
explain: The AI Office represents the EU in the international safety-institute network; the Hiroshima Process produced the G7 voluntary code for advanced AI developers; the OECD hosts definitions and metrics.

q: Open-source AI in EU policy is treated as:
b: Favoured with targeted exemptions (AI Act GPAI documentation relief unless systemic-risk) and seen as an ecosystem asset, though obligations return for systemic-risk models
explain: The Act balances openness benefits against frontier-risk: open-weight models get documentation relief but keep copyright/training-summary duties, and lose relief entirely at systemic-risk scale.

q: Which pairing of instrument → primary object is correct?
a: DGA → platform moderation; DSA → data intermediaries
b: DMA → gatekeeper contestability; NIS2 → organisational cybersecurity; CRA → product cybersecurity; Data Act → connected-product data access
c: CRA → AI conformity; AI Act → chip subsidies
explain: The acquis map in one line — the exam's favourite 'which law does what' pattern. DGA = data-sharing trust framework; DSA = platform duties.

q: An EU agency wants to deploy a high-risk AI system for visa application triage. Before first use it must, among other things:
b: Complete a FRIA (Art 27), ensure registration checks, and operate under EDPS supervision as its surveillance authority
explain: Public bodies deploying Annex III systems carry the FRIA duty; for EU institutions the EDPS supervises. Migration/border is Annex III area 7 — a realistic institutional scenario.

q: The AI Office's five units cover which portfolio areas?
b: Excellence in AI & Robotics; Regulation & Compliance; AI Safety; AI Innovation & Policy Coordination; AI for Societal Good
explain: The Office combines enforcement (Regulation & Compliance, AI Safety) with promotion (Excellence, Innovation, Societal Good) — mirroring the EU's twin-track 'trustworthy AI + competitiveness' strategy.

q: Which is TRUE about AI Act penalties and the GPAI Code of Practice?
a: Signing the Code is legally mandatory
b: Signing is voluntary; signatories get a recognised route to demonstrate compliance and reduced administrative scrutiny, while non-signatories must prove compliance by other means
d: The Code replaces the Act for signatories
explain: The Commission confirmed the Code as an adequate voluntary compliance tool (Aug 2025); some major providers signed, others (e.g. Meta) declined — both paths remain legal.

q: The EU's public-sector interoperability framework for digital government is anchored by:
b: The Data Act
explain: The Interoperable Europe Act (2024) sets mandatory interoperability assessments and the Interoperable Europe Board for cross-border digital public services — the GovTech layer AI-in-government sits on.

q: eIDAS 2.0 (Reg. (EU) 2024/1183) introduced:
b: The European Digital Identity Wallet, to be offered by every Member State, for cross-border identification and credential sharing
explain: EUDI Wallets (due to citizens by end-2026) underpin trusted digital transactions — identity infrastructure relevant to AI-era authentication and age verification debates.

q: The EU's 2026 CJEU referrals of several Member States (Ireland, Spain, France, Netherlands) concerned failure to transpose:
b: NIS2
explain: Trap alignment: the AI Act is a regulation (no transposition needed); NIS2 is a directive and its missed transposition triggered the July 2026 referrals.

q: Which EU institution formally adopts EPSO-relevant AI legislation like the AI Act?
b: The European Parliament and the Council, as co-legislators under the ordinary legislative procedure, on a Commission proposal
explain: Ordinary legislative procedure: Commission proposes, Parliament and Council co-decide. The Commission then adopts delegated/implementing acts (e.g. Annex III updates, Scientific Panel rules).

q: The Commission may amend Annex III (high-risk use cases) via:
a: A new full regulation each time
b: Delegated acts, adding or modifying use cases within the Act's defined areas based on risk evidence
explain: Art 7 empowers delegated acts to keep the high-risk list current — the mechanism that makes the Act adaptive without reopening the legislative procedure.

q: 'AI factories antennas' and gigafactory site selection in 2026 are run under:
b: EuroHPC JU calls, following its mandate extension to AI infrastructure and the official gigafactory call of July 2026
explain: The EuroHPC gigafactory call (30 July 2026) operationalises InvestAI: sites hosting ~100k+ advanced AI processors for training frontier-scale models in the EU.

q: The EU's position on general-purpose AI and copyright currently rests on:
b: The DSM Directive's TDM exceptions (Arts 3-4) plus AI Act Art 53 duties (copyright policy, training-content summary) — with court cases and a possible review ongoing
c: Full exemption of AI training from copyright
explain: No dedicated AI-copyright instrument exists; the TDM opt-out + transparency duties carry the load while litigation and policy review continue — an active, examinable policy frontier.

q: Which statement about AI and EU competition policy is accurate?
b: The Commission scrutinises AI partnerships and acquisitions (e.g. big-tech/model-lab alliances) under merger and antitrust tools, and the DMA can reach AI services integrated into gatekeeper platforms
c: AI companies are exempt from merger control
d: Only national authorities act on AI
explain: Competition policy is the fourth leg of EU AI governance: reviewing partnerships without formal mergers, cloud-compute dependencies, and DMA coverage as AI integrates into core platform services.

q: The 'twin transition' in EU policy language couples:
a: Digital and green transformations, with AI expected to contribute to both competitiveness and sustainability goals
b: Public and private sectors
explain: Digital + green is the standing Commission frame; AI's energy footprint vs its optimisation potential (energy grids, materials) is a common essay/MCQ angle.

q: Which funding programme most directly finances deployment-oriented AI capacity (testing facilities, skills, data spaces)?
b: The Digital Europe Programme (DIGITAL)
explain: DIGITAL funds AI testing and experimentation facilities, EDIHs, skills and data spaces; Horizon Europe covers research; both feed the AI Continent agenda.

q: European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs) are:
b: A network of one-stop shops helping SMEs and public administrations test and adopt digital and AI technologies, co-funded by DIGITAL
explain: 200+ EDIHs provide test-before-invest, skills and financing guidance — the retail layer of EU AI adoption policy, complementing AI Factories' compute layer.

q: As of late 2026, the accurate one-line summary of AI Act implementation status is:
b: Prohibitions, GPAI rules, governance and transparency apply; high-risk obligations are deferred (Annex III to Dec 2027, Annex I to Aug 2028) by the Digital Omnibus; standards and national authority designations are still catching up
explain: The status-quo snapshot an examiner would expect a candidate to hold in September 2026 — staged application plus simplification, not retreat.
